rationale: A wins because it keeps three clean, pitchable shapes and refuses to decorate the gaps. Its strongest angle, "Instacart's ad business hit a $1B run rate while its core delivery growth fell to single digits," is a real markets story with the proof burden named. B has useful instincts, but "The carts that skip checkout could be feeding the ad engine that just crossed $1 billion" is the kind of speculative connective tissue that gets a founder into trouble if the fact isn't nailed down first.
gaps_in_A: "Over 6,000 brands now advertise on a grocery-delivery app — what that says about retail media" needs outside benchmarks before it is more than a big-number wrapper; A knows this, but the angle is still thin without them.
"Caper smart carts let shoppers skip the checkout line — and they're spreading to more chains" risks being product news unless a named chain or operating result exists.
"Decay: 24hr" on the smart-cart rollout may be too harsh if the expansion is still unnamed and ongoing; the urgency is not actually proven.
A could have separated privacy/data implications as a watch item, but only if framed as an unconfirmed question, not a pitchable angle.
gaps_in_B: "The carts that skip checkout could be feeding the ad engine that just crossed $1 billion" infers a data link the update does not give. B flags the hole, but still elevates it to a full angle before it earns that seat.
"More grocery chains are letting Instacart's smart carts run their checkout line" overstates the fact; the carts help shoppers skip checkout, they do not necessarily "run" the checkout line.
"Instacart's smart-cart rollout turns it into checkout infrastructure for grocery chains" partially duplicates the store-operations smart-cart angle, just at a higher altitude.
"a spokesperson quote confirming that advertising is becoming the primary growth engine" is weak proof. A reporter needs revenue mix and growth data, not a quote blessing the thesis.
